Country.evidence_source: McKenzie et al.'s (2005) study of suicides within mental health services in the UK identified suicide clusters which were linked in both time and space.

Population.warning: The study focuses on 'case study deaths' of 'students' and uses 'informants' to convey information about them, suggesting a psychological autopsy approach. However, the gender of the deceased students is not specified, preventing the use of 'Bereaved (Male Suicide)' or 'Bereaved (Mixed)' as per the strict rules for Population extraction.

Area.evidence_source: Six of the students had experienced the break-up of a relationship shortly before their death; three were experiencing difficulties in a relationship and a further three students were described as experiencing unrequited love. A number of these relationships were described by friends or parents as 'turbulent' or 'emotionally charged'. Informants conveyed a picture of young people with limited experiences of intimate relationships struggling to manage the emotional vulnerability and losses they experienced: Two of the students who died had expressed doubts about their sexuality and these appeared to be a major source of uncertainty and distress for them. Suicide transmission (the term is used here in preference to the term 'suicide contagion') was a feature of four of the case study deaths. In two cases, the deaths of students included in the study occurred soon after or close to the anniversary of the suicide of a close friend. In another case, a friend of the student who was included in the research took their own life soon after: using the same method of death. In the fourth case, the student who died had had a relationship with another student who was described as attempting to take her own life on a number of occasions.
